summary: This comprehensive narrative review examines rapid eye movement (REM) sleep during early life in humans and mammals, arguing that abundant early REM sleep supports brain maturation as predicted by the ontogenetic sleep hypothesis. It describes how REM sleep amount, EEG, eye movements, breathing, heart rate and sleep-wake cycle timing change from preterm infancy through childhood. It then links early-life REM sleep disturbances to neurodevelopmental conditions including SIDS/SUID, narcolepsy, developmental disabilities, autism, ADHD and REM sleep behavior disorder, and begins a cross-species discussion of animal models.
one_line: A narrative review of how REM sleep changes across early human and mammalian development and how its disturbances relate to neurodevelopmental disorders.
key_facts: REM sleep in humans was first reported in adults in 1953 and was termed REM sleep by William Dement.
Between 28 and 30 weeks of gestation, most of a fetus's time is spent in REM sleep, with little signs of NREM sleep.
REM sleep is progressively reduced from 80% at 30 weeks to 67% between 33 and 35 weeks, and to 58% between 36 and 38 weeks.
Full-term newborns spend one-third of their day and one-half of their sleep in REM sleep.
REM sleep reaches a roughly stable proportion of 20% at about three years of age and remains approximately constant through childhood, adolescence and early adulthood.
In infants at 3 weeks of age, 60% of sleep periods begin with REM sleep, while at 6 months this is reduced to 20%.
During REM sleep, the respiratory rate is 18% greater than during NREM sleep, and mean heart rate is 3.4% higher.
In infants from 1 month to over 9 months of age, mean respiratory rate during REM sleep decreases from 35.8 to 22.3 breaths/min.
Every year in the USA, approximately 3500 infants die suddenly and unexpectedly.
SIDS was first defined in 1969, and the majority of sudden infant deaths are thought to occur during a narrow developmental window of postnatal 1–6 months.
Narcolepsy is due to a deficiency of hypothalamic hypocretin/orexin and more than 50% of disease onsets occur in childhood before puberty.
ADHD affects around 63 million children worldwide, and sleep problems have been found in around 55% of children diagnosed with ADHD.
Approximately 0.5 to 1.25 percent of the general population may suffer from REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD).
Premature neonates with more rapid eye movements during REM sleep have a better cognitive outcome at 6 months than those with fewer.
The ontogenetic sleep hypothesis suggests that REM sleep is ontogenetically primitive and plays an imperative role in maturation of the central nervous system.

entities.name: William Dement
entities.role: researcher who termed the sleep state associated with rapid eye movements REM sleep

entities.name: Roffwarg
entities.role: researcher who recorded full-term newborn sleep using polysomnography for 4 hours

entities.name: Blumberg
entities.role: researcher who concluded that myoclonic twitches during early life REM sleep contribute to establishment of the sensorimotor system

entities.name: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS)
entities.role: infant sleep death condition discussed as a neurodevelopmental disorder linked to REM sleep disturbances

entities.name: Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID)
entities.role: term for unexplained sudden death of an infant under 1 year old

entities.name: Narcolepsy
entities.role: neurological disorder with excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy and intrusions of REM sleep

entities.name: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
entities.role: common neurodevelopmental disorder with shorter REM sleep latency and sleep problems

entities.name: Autistic spectrum disorders (ASD)
entities.role: developmental disability associated with fewer and briefer episodes of REM sleep

entities.name: REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD)
entities.role: adult parasomnia resembling early-life REM sleep motor activity

entities.name: International Classification of Sleep Disorders (ICSD) 3rd Edition
entities.role: classification that divides narcolepsy into type 1 and type 2
